opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a more complicated question than people sometimes assume. On one hand, if you believe, as I do, that transformative AI could arrive this century, and possibly fairly soon, then it's plausibly the most important thing happening. Helping it go well looks like an enormous lever. So in principle, money directed at AI safety, governance, and related work could be extraordinarily valuable.

On the other hand, I'd caution people against assuming that donating is automatically the highest-impact thing they can do here. The field has gotten a meaningful amount of funding from large funders in recent years. So the binding constraint often isn't money. It's people: talented researchers, people who understand policy, people who can build organizations and exercise good judgment in a confusing, fast-moving area. If you could plausibly be one of those people, your time may matter a lot more than your dollars.

That said, I don't think the answer is "donations don't matter." There are a few cases where I think giving can be especially valuable.

One is funding things that big funders are poorly positioned to fund. That might be because a project is too small to be worth a large funder's attention, or because there are conflict-of-interest issues. It might also be politically awkward for a major foundation, or it might benefit from a diversity of funding sources so it isn't dependent on one institution. Political and policy-related giving is a good example, since some of it can't come from a foundation at all.

A second is if you have genuinely good judgment or unusual information about a particular opportunity. Maybe you know a specific researcher or a small group whose work you can evaluate better than an outside grantmaker could. Individual donors can sometimes move faster and take bets that institutions won't.

A third is simply that there's a lot of uncertainty about how much money the field will need going forward. If things heat up, if there are big policy windows or a need to scale up evaluation and security work quickly, the funding picture could change. So building up a willingness to give, and staying informed, has option value.

The thing I'd steer people away from is giving to anything with "AI" in the name and feeling like the box is checked. A lot of work in this space is neutral, and some is arguably counterproductive, for example work that mainly accelerates capabilities without much safety benefit. So I'd encourage people to be thoughtful, to look for advisors or funds that are seriously engaged with the specifics, and to think about where their money is actually additional.

So my overall take: it can be a very good use of money, but the bar for being thoughtful is high, and for many people the bigger question is whether they could contribute directly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one where my view has shifted a bit over time, and I want to be honest about the nuances rather than give a clean pitch.

The basic case is pretty simple. If you think AI could be one of the most important things to happen this century, and there's real work to be done to make that go well — alignment research, policy work, building the institutions that can respond when things get weird — then money is one of the inputs to that work, and it's an input a lot of people can provide even if they can't personally go do the research. That's the straightforward version.

But I'd add a few caveats. The first is that for a long time, I think the honest answer was that AI safety was not especially funding-constrained. Open Philanthropy and a few other funders had more money available than there were great things to spend it on. The bottleneck was people — specifically, people with the right skills and judgment who could actually run good projects. So if you asked me five or six years ago, I'd have said that for most people, the best thing you could do was probably to try to become one of those people, or to help find them, rather than to write checks.

I think that's changed somewhat. The field has grown a lot, there are more organizations that are actually ready to absorb money, and the ratio of good opportunities to available dollars has gotten a bit more balanced. So donating is more compelling now than it used to be. But I'd still say it's not the kind of thing where a marginal dollar is obviously going to be hugely impactful, because the big funders are still around and will fund a lot of the obvious stuff.

Where I think individual donors can really add value is in a few places. One is funding things that are too small or too early or too weird for a big institutional funder to bother with — a lot of good projects start as one person with an idea, and a relatively modest grant can get them off the ground. Another is funding things that are politically awkward for a large funder, or where a large funder's involvement would change the nature of the project. And a third is just diversity of judgment — I actually don't think it's healthy for one or two funders to be making all the calls about what gets supported, and having more independent decision-makers in the mix is a good thing in itself.

The other thing I'd say is that I don't think donating and doing direct work are really in tension for most people. If you're in a position to earn well and you're not going to switch into AI work directly, giving is a totally reasonable way to contribute, and you shouldn't feel like it's a second-class option. And if you are going to switch into direct work, you probably shouldn't be agonizing about donations anyway — your time and attention are the scarce thing.

So overall I'd say: it's a real way to contribute, it's gotten more compelling as the field has matured, but I'd go in with realistic expectations. You're probably not going to be the decisive dollar. You're more likely to be helping on the margins — supporting the long tail of smaller things, and adding some independent judgment to a space that could use more of it.

astra-6.text:
I think the case can be very strong, but it depends a lot on what you’re funding. “AI work” is a pretty broad category. The question is whether a particular organization has a plausible way to reduce risks from advanced AI, and whether additional money would actually help it do that.

One distinction I’d make is between thinking an issue is important and thinking there are great donation opportunities in that area. You can believe AI is enormously important and still find it difficult to identify a grant you feel good about. Some work is more constrained by finding the right people or having a clear research direction than by funding.

So I’d want to understand the specific opportunity: What will this donation make possible? Why is that useful? And why isn’t it already getting funded? I wouldn’t require certainty—we’re talking about a very uncertain area—but I would want a concrete account of how the money helps.

For someone who doesn’t want to spend a lot of time developing that judgment, finding a grantmaker whose reasoning they trust can make sense. But I don’t think the importance of AI, by itself, settles where you should donate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the case can be very strong, but it depends a lot on what you’re funding. “AI work” is an enormous category, and I wouldn’t assume that anything described as AI safety is therefore a good donation opportunity.

The basic case is that AI could be enormously consequential, and that there are things we can do now to improve the odds that it goes well. If you believe both of those things, then helping good people do useful work on that problem can be a very valuable contribution.

But there’s another question, which is: what does your additional dollar actually make happen? You might find a team with a promising research agenda that can’t get funding. Or you might find an organization whose main constraint is finding the right people, where more money doesn’t change very much. Those are very different situations.

So I’d distinguish being convinced that AI is important from being convinced that you’ve found a good giving opportunity. The former doesn’t automatically establish the latter. I’d want to understand the particular work, why it’s useful, and why funding is the thing that’s needed to make it happen.
